The Gospel of Union

Scope and honesty note. This study follows the relational gospel framework used throughout this series (the Trinitarian, union-centred reading associated with writers such as C. Baxter Kruger, building on earlier theologians like T. F. Torrance and the Greek Fathers). It does not quote Kruger verbatim. Where Christians genuinely disagree — the scope of "union," the meaning of new birth, justification, atonement — the disagreement is flagged in purple boxes. Word studies reflect standard lexicons; nuances vary among scholars. "Perichoresis" is a post-biblical term, and Part 1 says plainly what is and is not known about its origin.

PART 1 — The Triune Life: Perichoresis

1.1 What the Scriptures Show

The New Testament never uses the word perichoresis, but it describes the reality again and again: a life of mutual indwelling, love and honour between Father, Son and Spirit that existed before creation.

TextWhat it shows
John 1:1, 18The Word was pros ton theon — "toward / face to face with God"; the Son is "in the bosom (kolpos) of the Father," the place of closest intimacy.
John 14:10-11; 10:38"I am in the Father and the Father is in me" — mutual indwelling stated plainly.
John 5:19-20; 17:5, 24The Father loves the Son and shows him all; they share glory and love "before the foundation of the world."
John 16:14-15; 15:26The Spirit takes what is the Son's and declares it; he proceeds from the Father — the Spirit is inside the same circle of giving.
Matt 3:16-17; 28:19; 2 Cor 13:14The three appear together at the baptism, in the baptismal name, and in the apostolic blessing ("the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit").
1 John 4:8, 16"God is love" — which suggests, as classic theological reasoning argues, that love was never a thing God acquired by making creatures; it is what God eternally is.

1.2 The Word "Perichoresis": What Is and Isn't Known

PointDetail
The wordπεριχώρησις perichoresis, from peri ("around") + chorein ("to make room, to contain, to go forward"), related to chora ("space, room"). Core sense: mutual indwelling, interpenetration, making room around one another.
Where it comes fromNot in Scripture. Used first of the union of Christ's divine and human natures (traditionally credited to Gregory of Nazianzus, 4th century; also Maximus the Confessor), then applied to the three persons of the Trinity by John of Damascus (8th century). Latin: circumincessio (moving in and around); a variant circuminsessio (sitting in and around) arose from the similar sound.
The "dance"A link to choreia (χορεία), the Greek circle dance with song, is generally regarded by standard reference works as a modern wordplay, not grounded in Greek etymology or early Christian use. As an image, however, it has become a widely loved and fruitful metaphor (Moltmann; Kruger's The Great Dance) for a life of mutual giving, joy and movement.

How to use the dance image honestly. Say: "Perichoresis means mutual indwelling; the 'dance' is a picture of it, not the Greek meaning of the word." That keeps both the accuracy and the beauty.

1.3 The Dance in the Bible's Own Imagery (a Resonance, Not a Proof)

Scripture itself pictures joy in God's presence as dance: David dancing before the LORD (2 Sam 6:14), "praise his name with dancing" (Ps 149:3; 150:4), "then shall the young women rejoice in the dance" (Jer 31:13, machol), and, most strikingly, the Father's feast for the returned son, where the older brother hears "music and dancing" (Luke 15:25, choroi). The Father's house is a place of feasting and dancing; the question of the parable is whether we will come in.

1.4 Cultural Background: A Different Kind of God

In much ancient Greek philosophical thought the highest reality was imagined as solitary, self-sufficient and unmoved (Aristotle's "unmoved mover" contemplating itself); in the Greco-Roman pantheon the gods were quarrelsome and used humans for their own ends. Israel's God was already different — a covenant God who sees, hears and pursues (Exod 3:7-8). The Christian claim goes further: at the centre of reality is not a solitary self-contemplation but a communion of self-giving love. That is why "union" is not an add-on to the gospel: it is the shape of God's own life, offered.

PART 2 — Made for Participation

If God's life is a communion, the question is: what was creation for? Scripture's answer is that humanity was made to share it.

TextWhat it says about purpose
Gen 1:26-27"Let us make man in our image... male and female" — the image of a relational God is expressed in relationship.
Eph 1:3-6Blessed "in Christ"; chosen "in him before the foundation of the world"; destined for adoption — the plan precedes the fall; union is God's plan A.
Eph 1:9-10The mystery of his will: to gather up all things in Christ.
Col 1:15-20All things created through and for him, held together in him, reconciled through him.
John 17:21-26"That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us... that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
2 Pet 1:4"Partakers (koinonoi) of the divine nature."
Acts 17:27-28"He is not far from each one of us, for in him we live and move and have our being."

Participation is not a reward for getting everything right; it is why we exist. That reframes salvation: not "how do outsiders get in?" but "how do people living as though they were outside come to know where they are?"

PART 3 — The Lie of Separation

3.1 How the Lie Works

In Genesis 3 the serpent never asks Adam and Eve to hate God; he plants a picture of God as withholding ("Did God really say...?", "God knows that when you eat... you will be like God") — implying that life is something to be grasped apart from Him. The result is fear and hiding ("I was afraid... so I hid," 3:10), then the two fallen strategies of this series: self-salvation (the fig leaves) and escape (the trees). Every I-am-not ("not included, not loved, not safe") is a local version of one master lie: you are outside, and it is up to you.

3.2 Scripture's Counter-Evidence

TextWhat it says
Ps 139:7-12"Where shall I flee from your presence?" — there is nowhere to go.
Rom 8:35, 38-39"Who shall separate (χωρίζω chorizo) us from the love of Christ?... nothing... will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord."
John 14:18"I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
2 Cor 5:19"In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them."
Eph 2:13-18"You who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ... he himself is our peace... through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father."
Col 1:19-20Through him God reconciled to himself all things, making peace by the blood of his cross.
Heb 13:5"I will never leave you nor forsake you."

3.3 Alienation Is Real — but Where Does It Live?

Scripture does not deny alienation; it locates it. Notice the words:

TextWordingObservation
Col 1:21"You were once ἀπηλλοτριωμένους apellotriomenous (alienated) and hostile in mind (διάνοια dianoia), doing evil deeds."The alienation is described as in the mind, a state of hostility and estrangement — and then "he has now reconciled you" (v.22).
Eph 4:18"Darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them."Alienation tied to ignorance and a hardened heart.
Eph 2:12-13"Separated from Christ... having no hope and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near."Real condition; real remedy accomplished in Christ.
Isa 59:2"Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God."Sin produces real separation of fellowship and trust.

Reading these together (the framework's position): separation is real as experience, hostility of mind and broken trust, and it has real consequences. But it is a lie as the final truth about humanity, because God has not withdrawn and Christ has already brought humanity near. The lie is not that people feel far; the lie is that being far is what is true and permanent.

Where Christians differ. Many evangelical and Reformed readers hold that union with Christ is applied to individuals by the Spirit through faith, and that outside faith people are genuinely "without God" (Eph 2:12) and "children of wrath" (Eph 2:3). Union/inclusion readings hold that Christ's incarnation united him to all humanity, so that "in Christ" is the objective truth about everyone (appealing to texts such as 2 Cor 5:14-19; Eph 1:10; Col 1:20; Rom 5:18), and that faith is awakening into what is already true; writers in this stream differ on the final outcome for those who never awaken. Both sides affirm that the new birth, faith and growth are real and that no one is saved by their own effort. Readers should weigh the difference as a real one.

PART 4 — Union Accomplished and the "With" Words

4.1 How the Gospel Says Union Was Accomplished

MovementWhat happenedTexts
IncarnationThe Son takes our humanity — "the Word became flesh" — sharing flesh and blood and becoming our brother, so that what was assumed is healed.John 1:14; Phil 2:6-8; Heb 2:11-17
Cross"One has died for all, therefore all have died" — the old, alienated existence is taken to death in him.2 Cor 5:14-15; Rom 6:3-6; Gal 2:20
Resurrection and ascensionA new humanity raised and seated in the Father's presence.Eph 2:5-6; Col 3:1-3; Rom 6:4-5
Pentecost / the SpiritThe Spirit of the Son is sent into our hearts, making the Son's own relationship with the Father ours to share ("Abba").John 14:16-20; Gal 4:4-6; Rom 8:9-16

4.2 The "With" Words (the sun- prefix)

Paul's Greek is full of compounds beginning sun- ("with, together with"). Each says that what happened to Christ happened to us in him:

GreekMeaningText
συσταυρόω sustaurooCrucified withGal 2:20; Rom 6:6
συνθάπτω sunthaptoBuried withRom 6:4; Col 2:12
συζωοποιέω suzoopoieoMade alive together withEph 2:5; Col 2:13
συνεγείρω sunegeiroRaised together withEph 2:6; Col 2:12; 3:1
συγκαθίζω sunkathizoSeated together withEph 2:6
σύμφυτος sumphutosGrown together with, unitedRom 6:5
συγκληρονόμος sunkleronomosFellow heirRom 8:17
κολλάω kollaoTo be glued, joined to1 Cor 6:17 ("joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him")

The phrase "in Christ" or "in him" appears well over a hundred times in Paul's letters; in Ephesians 1 alone, blessing, choosing, redemption, inheritance and sealing are all "in him."
